title: How Debt Counselling Works in South Africa
excerpt: A plain-language walkthrough of what actually happens during formal debt review — from your first assessment to what protection it gives you along the way.

body.text: “Debt counselling” and “debt review” refer to the same formal process in South Africa — a legally regulated route under the National Credit Act (NCA), overseen by the National Credit Regulator (NCR), for consumers who are over-indebted. Knowing the actual shape of the process makes it much easier to decide whether it's right for you.
Step 1: You apply, in terms of section 86
A consumer who is struggling to pay their credit agreements applies for debt review under section 86 of the NCA. This is something you apply for — it isn't applied to you without your involvement.
Step 2: The debt counsellor has 30 business days to make a determination

The regulations give a debt counsellor 30 business days from receiving your application to determine whether you are over-indebted, or not yet over-indebted but likely to struggle to meet your obligations in time. They review your income, expenses and everything you owe to reach that determination.

An important nuance that's often misunderstood: the debt counsellor does not “declare” you over-indebted. They make a determination and refer it, with a proposal for how your debt could be restructured.
Step 3: A court declares over-indebtedness and grants the relief

It is the court that conducts a hearing, formally declares a consumer over-indebted, and grants debt relief by restructuring the credit agreement debt. This is why debt review carries real legal weight — and also why it follows a defined process rather than an instant fix.
Under section 79 of the NCA, over-indebtedness isn't only about being unable to pay right now; it also covers a future or imminent inability to meet your obligations.
Everyone involved must act in good faith

The NCA requires all parties to the debt review process — you, your credit providers, and the debt counsellor — to participate in good faith. Credit providers are not automatically obliged to accept a proposed plan, which is part of why the court route matters.
What protection you actually get

While you are under formal debt review and complying with your restructured plan, credit providers are restricted from taking further legal action on the debts covered by it. That protection is specific to formal debt review — it does not apply to informal debt mediation.
How it ends

Once you have satisfied all the obligations under every credit agreement covered by the re-arrangement, a debt counsellor issues a clearance certificate in terms of section 71. Its effect matters: the detail of the debt review is then expunged from the credit bureaus' records. Long-term agreements such as a mortgage bond are treated differently — section 71 allows an exit once the shorter-term restructured debts are settled, even where a bond is still being paid.
What it isn't

Debt review is not a new loan or a consolidation loan — you aren't borrowing more money, you're changing the terms of what you already owe. It also doesn't guarantee a specific lower interest rate or instalment; what changes depends on what's agreed or ordered.

items.q: How long does the debt counsellor have to assess my application?
items.a: The regulations allow 30 business days from receiving your application to make a determination on whether you are over-indebted.

items.q: Does the debt counsellor decide that I'm over-indebted?
items.a: No. The debt counsellor makes a determination and a proposal; it is the court that declares a consumer over-indebted and grants the restructuring.

items.q: Does debt counselling guarantee my interest rates will drop?
items.a: No. Any change depends on what is agreed with each credit provider or ordered by the court — it isn't a guaranteed outcome.

sources.title: National Credit Act 34 of 2005

title: Debt Review vs Debt Mediation: What's the Real Difference?
excerpt: Two different routes, often confused with each other. Here's what actually separates formal debt review from informal debt mediation — and how to think about which fits your situation.

body.text: If you're comparing your options, it helps to see debt review and debt mediation side by side rather than treating them as interchangeable — because legally and practically, they aren't.
Debt review: formal, regulated, with legal protection

Debt review is a formal process under the National Credit Act, regulated by the National Credit Regulator. A registered debt counsellor restructures all your credit agreements into one plan. While you comply with it, you get legal protection from further action on those debts — and if a credit provider won't agree to the proposed plan, there's a route through the courts or the National Consumer Tribunal.
Debt mediation: informal, flexible, no statutory protection

Debt mediation is a negotiation, conducted account by account, outside that formal legal framework. It can be a reasonable option in some situations, but it comes with a real trade-off: there's no statutory protection. A creditor can decline your proposal, and can still pursue legal action against you during the negotiation.
So which one is “better”?

Neither is universally better — they solve different problems. Debt review suits people who need the legal protection and are prepared to work within a regulated, structured process. Debt mediation may suit people whose situation doesn't require (or doesn't qualify for) that level of formal intervention. This is exactly the kind of thing worth discussing with a consultant before deciding, rather than guessing from a comparison article alone.

items.q: Can I switch from debt mediation to debt review later?
items.a: That depends on your specific situation and would need a fresh assessment — it isn't automatic.

items.q: Does debt mediation affect my credit record the way debt review does?
items.a: The two processes are recorded differently. Speak to a consultant about how each would specifically affect your credit record.

title: How to Build a Realistic Monthly Budget
excerpt: A budget only works if it reflects what actually happens in your bank account. Here's a straightforward way to build one you can stick to.

body.text: Most budgets fail for a boring reason: they're built around what someone thinks their spending should look like, not what it actually is. A realistic budget starts with real numbers.
1. Start with take-home pay, not gross salary
Use what actually lands in your account after tax and deductions — that's the number you can genuinely work with, not your salary on paper.
2. List fixed essentials first
Rent or bond, transport to work, groceries, utilities, insurance, and minimum debt repayments. These are the costs that don't flex much month to month — get an honest total before anything else.
3. Track variable spending for one real month

Eating out, subscriptions, incidental purchases — these are usually where a budget quietly falls apart. Look at an actual bank statement rather than estimating from memory; most people underestimate this category significantly.
4. Compare income to total outgoings honestly

If essentials plus debt repayments already exceed your income, that's important information — not a failure on your part, but a sign that your current repayment structure may not be sustainable, and worth an honest conversation with a consultant rather than a stricter budget alone.
5. Revisit it monthly, not once
A budget is a working document. Income and expenses shift — a new account, a rent increase, a change in hours. Treat it as something you check in on regularly, not a one-time exercise.
Our free budget calculator can help you get a clear picture of where you stand in a few minutes — you don't need to share any contact details to see the results.

items.q: Is the budget calculator the same as a debt review assessment?
items.a: No. It gives you a general budget summary, not a formal debt review proposal or a personalised repayment estimate — that requires a full assessment.

items.q: Is my information from the calculator stored anywhere?
items.a: No. The figures stay in your browser for that session and aren't saved on our servers unless you separately submit a callback request.

title: Understanding Your Credit Profile
excerpt: Your credit profile affects more than loan approvals. Here's what it actually reflects, and what does (and doesn't) show up on it during debt review.

body.text: Your credit profile is a record, held by registered credit bureaus, of how you've managed credit over time — accounts, repayment history and any adverse listings. Credit providers use it to assess applications, but it's also simply a picture of your own financial history, and you have specific rights over it.
You are entitled to one free credit report a year

Under the National Credit Act, you may request your credit report from the credit bureaus once every twelve months at no cost. If you haven't looked at yours recently, that's a free and genuinely useful place to start — you can't fix what you can't see.
Disputing something that's wrong is also free

If information on your report is incorrect, you can lodge a dispute with the credit bureau to have it investigated and corrected. You do not pay the credit bureau to challenge information or to correct your profile. The Credit Ombud also resolves disputes between consumers and subscribing members of the non-bank credit industry, including credit bureaus, free of charge.
This matters because it's exactly the space where some businesses charge large fees for something you are entitled to do yourself at no cost.
What affects your profile
Missed or late payments, the number and type of accounts you hold, how long you've held credit, and formal processes such as debt review or court judgments are all reflected over time.
Debt review and your credit record

Being under formal debt review is reflected on your credit record for the duration of the process. This is a normal part of how the system works. When you complete the process and a clearance certificate is issued under section 71 of the NCA, the detail of that debt review must be expunged from the credit bureaus' records.
Be cautious of paid “fast removal” offers

The NCR has publicly warned consumers about businesses promising fast debt review removal for a large upfront fee. Under section 126A(3) of the National Credit Act, a business offering to help remove information from your credit record generally cannot take payment from you before that service has actually been carried out. If an offer sounds like a guaranteed shortcut, treat it carefully.

items.q: How often can I get my credit report for free?
items.a: The National Credit Act entitles you to request your credit report from the credit bureaus once every twelve months at no cost.

items.q: Does it cost money to fix a mistake on my credit report?
items.a: No. You do not pay the credit bureau to lodge a dispute or to have incorrect information corrected, and the Credit Ombud's dispute service is free.

items.q: Can my income improving alone get me removed from debt review?
items.a: No. Removal follows specific legal routes and requires an assessment — an improved income alone doesn't automatically qualify you.

title: What to Do When You Can't Afford Your Monthly Repayments
excerpt: Struggling to keep up with repayments is more common than it feels. Here's a clear-headed way to work out what's actually going on, and what your options are.

body.text: If your repayments no longer fit comfortably alongside your living costs, the most useful first step isn't panic or avoidance — it's getting an honest, specific picture of your numbers.
1. Get a real total, not an estimate

List every debt, its monthly repayment, and your actual take-home income and essential expenses. It's uncomfortable, but a vague sense of “it's tight” makes it much harder to find the right next step than a specific number does.
2. Understand that you have more than one option

Depending on your situation, that might mean formal debt review (with legal protection, but a regulated process to follow), informal debt mediation (more flexible, but without statutory protection), or simply restructuring your own budget first. There isn't one correct answer that applies to everyone — it depends on your specific numbers.
3. Don't wait for the situation to get worse before acting

The earlier a genuinely unaffordable repayment structure is addressed, the more options tend to be available. Waiting until accounts are significantly in arrears narrows what can realistically be done.
4. Be cautious of guaranteed outcomes

Any legitimate assessment of your situation should be able to explain what depends on your circumstances and what depends on individual creditors agreeing to something — not promise a specific reduced payment or interest rate before that's actually been worked out.
5. Talk to someone before choosing a path
A short conversation with a consultant, working from your real numbers, is a far better basis for a decision than guessing between debt review and debt mediation from general information alone.

items.q: Will speaking to a consultant commit me to anything?
items.a: No. Requesting a callback is an enquiry, not a commitment — a consultant reviews your request and contacts you to talk through your situation.

title: How to Deal With Multiple Creditors at Once
excerpt: Owing several different creditors makes everything feel more chaotic than it needs to. Here's how to bring some order to it before deciding what to do next.

body.text: When debt is spread across several credit providers — a credit card here, a store account there, a personal loan somewhere else — it's easy to lose track of the overall picture. That's usually the first problem worth solving, before deciding on a strategy.
1. Build one single list

Every account, its outstanding balance, its minimum monthly repayment, and who it's with. Scattered across statements and apps, this information is hard to act on; in one place, patterns become obvious — which accounts are largest, which are most urgent, which are manageable.
2. Understand the difference between restructuring and consolidating

Formal debt review restructures your existing repayments into a single, revised monthly plan — it is not a new loan or a consolidation loan product. That distinction matters: you're not taking on new debt to pay off old debt, you're changing the terms of what you already owe.
3. Know that creditors don't have to agree to everything

Whether you're pursuing formal debt review or informal debt mediation, a credit provider isn't automatically obliged to accept a proposed plan. Under debt review, unresolved disputes have a route through the courts or the National Consumer Tribunal; under debt mediation, a creditor can simply decline.
4. A single combined plan doesn't remove complexity overnight

Even once a restructured plan is in place, it still needs to be maintained — consistent payments, kept up over time. It simplifies the structure of what you owe, but doesn't remove the need for an ongoing, realistic budget alongside it.

items.q: Is a combined repayment plan the same as a consolidation loan?
items.a: No. Restructuring your repayments through debt review is not a new loan — it's a revised repayment plan across your existing credit agreements.

title: Common Debt Mistakes to Avoid
excerpt: Some of the most common ways a manageable debt situation becomes a harder one — and how to steer around them.

body.text: Avoiding the problem instead of assessing it

It's a natural response to avoid looking closely at a stressful number, but avoidance tends to narrow your options over time rather than protect you. An honest, early assessment usually leaves more paths open than waiting does.
Trusting a guarantee that sounds too clean

Be cautious of anyone promising a specific reduced interest rate, a fast debt review removal, or a guaranteed outcome before actually assessing your situation. The National Credit Regulator has specifically warned about businesses charging large upfront fees for promised fast removal from debt review — and under the National Credit Act, that kind of service generally can't be paid for upfront before it's actually delivered.
Confusing debt review with a new loan

Debt review restructures your existing repayments — it isn't a consolidation loan, and you're not borrowing new money to solve the problem. Going into it expecting a loan product can lead to real confusion about what's actually happening to your finances.
Assuming debt mediation gives the same protection as debt review

They're genuinely different: formal debt review carries legal protection from further action while you comply, with an escalation route through the courts or the National Consumer Tribunal if a creditor won't agree. Debt mediation doesn't carry that statutory protection — a creditor can decline a proposal or still pursue legal action during the negotiation.
Not revisiting your budget once a plan is in place

A restructured repayment plan only works alongside a realistic budget that's kept up to date. Income and expenses change — treating the plan as “set and forget” is one of the more common ways people fall behind again.

items.q: If I've made one of these mistakes already, is it too late?
items.a: No — these are common, and a consultant can help you understand your current situation and realistic next steps, regardless of what's already happened.

title: Prescribed Debt: When a Debt Becomes Too Old to Claim
excerpt: South African law puts a time limit on most ordinary debts. Here's what “prescribed debt” means, why acknowledging an old debt can restart the clock, and what collectors may not do.

sources.title: Prescription Act 68 of 1969
Prescription of Debt in the Consumer-Credit Industry [2019] PER 51
National Credit Act 34 of 2005
Promise to pay — prolonging prescription [2013] DEREBUS 128

body.text: If an old debt resurfaces years later — a store account you'd forgotten, a call from a collector about something from a previous job — it's worth knowing that South African law puts a time limit on most ordinary debts. The term for this is prescription.
The three-year rule

Section 11(d) of the Prescription Act 68 of 1969 sets a prescription period of three years for ordinary debts, which includes most consumer credit debt. Once a debt has prescribed, it is extinguished, and a collector cannot successfully sustain a claim on it.

Not every debt falls under the three-year period — some categories, such as mortgage bonds and judgment debts, have longer periods. This is one of the reasons it's worth getting a proper view of a specific debt rather than assuming.
What the National Credit Act adds

Section 126B of the National Credit Act specifically regulates practices around prescribed consumer debts — including prohibiting the sale of prescribed consumer debt, and the continued collection or re-activation of it. In other words, this isn't only a technical defence you have to raise: there are rules about what may be done with these debts in the first place.
The trap: acknowledging the debt can restart the clock

This is the part that catches people out. If you acknowledge the debt — for example by promising to pay, agreeing to a payment arrangement, or making a payment towards it — prescription can be interrupted and the period can begin running again. A collector asking you to “just pay something small to show good faith” on a very old debt may be doing exactly that.
So if you're contacted about a debt you believe is very old, the safer move is to ask for the details in writing and get advice before agreeing to anything or making a payment.
What this doesn't mean

Prescription is not a strategy for dealing with current debt. It applies to debts that have already run their course untouched — it is not a way to avoid debts you are actively repaying or that are still within their period. If you're struggling with current repayments, that's a different problem with different solutions, such as debt review.
What to do if you think a debt has prescribed

Ask the collector for the full details of the debt in writing, including when the last payment or acknowledgement was made. Check your credit report — you're entitled to one free copy a year — to see what is actually listed against your name. Then get advice specific to that debt before responding, because the consequences of a casual acknowledgement are real.

items.q: How long before an ordinary debt prescribes in South Africa?
items.a: Section 11(d) of the Prescription Act 68 of 1969 sets three years for ordinary debts. Some categories, such as mortgage bonds and judgment debts, have longer periods.

items.q: Can paying a small amount restart the clock on an old debt?
items.a: It can. Acknowledging a debt — including by making a payment or agreeing to a payment arrangement — can interrupt prescription so that the period starts running again.

items.q: Is a prescribed debt still collectable?
items.a: A prescribed debt is extinguished and will not support a claim, and the National Credit Act restricts selling, collecting or re-activating prescribed consumer debt.

title: Your Rights With Credit Bureaus (And What They Cost: Nothing)
excerpt: You can see your credit report free once a year, dispute mistakes at no cost, and escalate to a free ombud. Here's how to use rights you already have.

sources.title: You are entitled to a free credit report
National Credit Act 34 of 2005
Notebook on the National Credit Act, 2005
sources.publisher: Department of Trade, Industry and Competition

body.text: A surprising number of people pay for things the National Credit Act already gives them for free. If your credit record matters to you — and it does if you're planning to apply for anything, or recovering from a difficult period — these are the rights worth knowing.
1. One free credit report every twelve months

The National Credit Act entitles you to request your credit report from the credit bureaus once every twelve months at no cost. Your report sets out your borrowing and repayment history and gives you a view of your current credit status — including accounts you may have forgotten about.
2. Disputing incorrect information is free

If something on your report is wrong, you can lodge a dispute with the credit bureau to have it investigated and corrected. You do not pay the credit bureau to challenge information or to have your profile corrected. There is no need to pay a third party for the act of lodging a dispute itself.
3. The Credit Ombud is free too

The Credit Ombud is a recognised industry ombud scheme that resolves disputes between consumers and subscribing members of the non-bank credit industry, including credit providers and credit bureaus. Its services are free to consumers. If a dispute with a bureau isn't resolved properly, that's an escalation route available to you.
Why this matters for “debt review removal” offers

Knowing these rights makes it much easier to judge an offer. Under section 126A(3) of the National Credit Act, a business offering to help remove information from your credit record generally cannot take payment from you before that service has actually been carried out. Combined with the fact that disputes themselves are free, a large upfront fee for a promised quick fix deserves real scepticism.

That's not to say legitimate help doesn't exist — exiting debt review properly, for example, follows defined legal routes and can genuinely require professional assistance. The point is that you should know what you're paying for, and what you could do yourself at no cost.
A sensible order to do this in

Get your free report first. Read it properly and note anything that looks wrong or unfamiliar. Dispute genuine errors directly with the bureau. Then, if you need help with your actual debt position rather than with the record itself, speak to a consultant about your options.

items.q: How do I get my free credit report?
items.a: Request it from a registered credit bureau. The National Credit Act entitles you to one free report every twelve months.

items.q: Do I have to pay someone to fix an error on my credit report?
items.a: No. Lodging a dispute with the credit bureau to correct incorrect information is free, and the Credit Ombud's dispute service is also free to consumers.

items.q: Can a company charge me upfront to remove information from my credit record?
items.a: Under section 126A(3) of the National Credit Act, a business offering that service generally cannot take payment from you before the service has actually been carried out.

title: What Documents Do I Need for Debt Review?
excerpt: A practical checklist of what a debt counsellor typically asks for, why each item is needed, and what to do if you're self-employed or missing something.

sources.title: National Credit Act 34 of 2005
National Credit Act: Regulations: Debt counselling
Notebook on the National Credit Act, 2005
sources.publisher: Department of Trade, Industry and Competition

body.text: Gathering paperwork is the part of debt review people most often stall on. It helps to know that almost everything asked for exists to answer one question: what can you genuinely afford each month? A debt counsellor has to make a determination about whether you are over-indebted, and that determination has to rest on real figures rather than estimates.

The exact list can vary between debt counsellors and depending on your circumstances. Confirm the specific requirements with the consultant handling your application — but the categories below are what you should expect to be asked for.
Proof of identity

A copy of your South African ID (smart card or green barcoded book). If you're married in community of property, your spouse's details normally matter too, because the joint estate affects the assessment.
Proof of income

If you're employed, recent payslips — usually the last three months. If your income varies (commission, overtime, seasonal work), a longer period gives a fairer picture of what you actually earn on average rather than in a good month.

If you're self-employed, you won't have payslips, and that's expected. Instead you'd typically provide business bank statements, recent financial statements or management accounts, and any drawings records showing what you actually take out of the business. If you're paid in cash, say so early — it changes what evidence is realistic, and it's better dealt with upfront than discovered later.
Bank statements

Usually the last three months for every account you use. These matter more than most people expect: they show what actually leaves your account, including debit orders you may have forgotten and expenses you'd underestimate from memory. A budget built on guesses tends to collapse in month two.
Details of every credit agreement

For each debt: who the credit provider is, the account number, the outstanding balance, and the current monthly instalment. Recent statements or letters are ideal. Your credit report is useful here too — you're entitled to one free copy every twelve months, and it will surface accounts you may have lost track of.
Proof of residence and living expenses

A recent utility bill or lease. You'll also be asked to set out monthly living costs — rent or bond, transport, groceries, school fees, insurance, municipal charges. Be realistic rather than optimistic: understating your expenses produces a repayment plan you cannot actually keep.
“What if I'm missing something?”

Start the conversation anyway. Missing one document rarely stops an application outright; it usually just needs to be replaced with an equivalent, or followed up. Waiting months to apply because one payslip is missing is the more costly choice — the assessment can often begin while you retrieve the rest.
A note on what documents do not do

Submitting documents doesn't mean you qualify. The paperwork enables an assessment; the assessment determines whether you are over-indebted, and under the National Credit Act a court ultimately grants the restructuring. Anyone promising an outcome before seeing your numbers is not describing the real process.

items.q: How many months of bank statements are needed?
items.a: Typically the last three months for each account you use, though a longer period may be requested if your income varies. Confirm the exact requirement with the consultant handling your application.

items.q: What if I'm self-employed and have no payslip?
items.a: That's expected. Business bank statements, financial statements or management accounts and drawings records are normally used instead. Mention it early so the right evidence is requested from the start.

items.q: Does submitting documents mean I qualify for debt review?
items.a: No. The documents allow an assessment of whether you are over-indebted. That determination, and the court order that restructures the debt, come after.

title: What Happens After You Apply for Debt Review?
excerpt: The stages between submitting your application and having a restructured repayment plan — including who decides what, and roughly how long each part takes.

sources.title: National Credit Act 34 of 2005
National Credit Act: Regulations: Debt counselling
Unintentionally Trapped by Debt Review [2019] PER 69
Circular 6 of 2017: Interpretation of section 71 of the NCA

body.text: Applying is the start of a defined legal process, not a single event. Knowing the sequence makes the waiting far less stressful, because you can tell the difference between a normal gap and something that has actually stalled.
1. Your application is received and creditors are notified
Once you apply under section 86 of the National Credit Act, your credit providers and the credit bureaus are notified that you have applied for debt review. This is what begins the formal process.
2. The affordability assessment (up to 30 business days)

The regulations give the debt counsellor 30 business days from receiving your application to make a determination: are you over-indebted, or not yet over-indebted but likely to struggle to meet your obligations in time? This is where your income, expenses and debts are worked through properly.
An important point that is widely misunderstood: the debt counsellor does not declare you over-indebted. They make a determination and prepare a proposal for how your debts could be restructured.
3. A proposal goes to your credit providers

The proposed restructured plan is put to the credit providers. They are not automatically obliged to accept it. The National Credit Act requires all parties — you, the credit providers and the debt counsellor — to participate in good faith, but agreement is not guaranteed.
4. The matter goes to court

It is the court that conducts a hearing, formally declares a consumer over-indebted, and grants relief by restructuring the credit agreement debt. This step is what gives debt review its legal weight — and it is also why the process takes longer than an informal arrangement.
5. You pay according to the plan

Once an arrangement or order is in place, you make a single monthly payment which is distributed to your credit providers. While you are complying, credit providers are restricted from taking further legal action on the debts covered by the plan.
6. Completion

When you have satisfied the obligations under the agreements covered by the re-arrangement, a clearance certificate is issued under section 71, and the detail of the debt review is expunged from the credit bureaus' records. Long-term debt such as a home loan is treated differently — section 71 allows an exit once the shorter-term restructured debts are settled, even where a bond continues.
How long does the whole thing take?

The assessment stage has a defined window (30 business days). The stages after that depend on creditor responses and court rolls, which is why no one can honestly quote you a single fixed timeline at the outset. Be cautious of anyone who does.

items.q: How long does the affordability assessment take?
items.a: The regulations allow the debt counsellor 30 business days from receiving the application to make a determination.

items.q: Can creditors still contact me during the process?
items.a: Once you are under debt review and complying with the arrangement, credit providers are restricted from taking further legal action on the debts covered by it. If something feels wrong, raise it with your debt counsellor.

items.q: Is there a guaranteed timeline for the whole process?
items.a: No. Only the assessment stage has a set window. The rest depends on creditor responses and court processes.

title: Can Debt Review Be Removed or Terminated?
excerpt: “Removal” means different things at different stages. Here's what actually applies — and why anyone guaranteeing a quick exit for a fee deserves scrutiny.

sources.title: National Credit Act 34 of 2005
Circular 6 of 2017: Interpretation of section 71 of the NCA
Explanatory Note to the Withdrawal Guidelines
Unintentionally Trapped by Debt Review [2019] PER 69

body.text: When people ask about “removing debt review” they usually mean one of several quite different things. The honest answer depends entirely on which one applies to you, and on what stage you are at.
What people usually mean

items: “I've finished paying and I want the debt review flag off my credit record.”
“I applied, but I've changed my mind and it hasn't gone to court yet.”
“My circumstances improved and I can afford my original instalments again.”
“I'm already under a court order and I want out.”

body.text: If you have completed the process

This is the cleanest route. Once the debts covered by your re-arrangement are satisfied, a registered debt counsellor issues a clearance certificate under section 71 of the National Credit Act, and the detail of the debt review must then be expunged from the credit bureaus' records.
If a court order is already in place

Exiting before the debts are settled is a different matter, and generally requires a court application. Removal follows specific legal routes — an improved income on its own does not automatically qualify you, and there is no administrative shortcut that bypasses the order.
If your circumstances have genuinely changed

A change in income doesn't automatically end debt review, but it is a legitimate reason to have your situation reassessed. What is available to you depends on your stage in the process and what the court order (if any) says.
The warning worth taking seriously

The National Credit Regulator has publicly warned consumers about businesses promising fast debt review removal in exchange for a large upfront fee. Under section 126A(3) of the National Credit Act, a business offering to help remove information from your credit record generally cannot take payment from you before that service has actually been carried out.
So: be sceptical of a guaranteed outcome quoted before anyone has looked at your file, and be especially sceptical of a large fee demanded upfront for that promise.
What an honest answer looks like

Anyone dealing with this properly should ask what stage you are at, whether an order exists, and what your current position with creditors is — before telling you what's possible. If someone tells you removal is simple without asking any of that, they are not describing your actual situation.

items.q: Can I be removed from debt review just because I can afford my payments again?
items.a: No. Removal follows specific legal routes and requires an assessment. An improved income alone doesn't automatically qualify you.

items.q: Can a company guarantee they'll remove me from debt review?
items.a: Treat guarantees with caution. The NCR has warned about businesses promising fast removal for large upfront fees, and s126A(3) of the NCA generally prohibits taking payment before such a service is actually carried out.

items.q: What is a clearance certificate?
items.a: The document a registered debt counsellor issues once the debts covered by your re-arrangement are paid in full. It's used to update your status with the credit bureaus.

title: How Inflation Affects Household Debt
excerpt: Inflation quietly changes what your salary covers. Here's the mechanism, in plain language, and what it means if you're already repaying debt.

sources.title: Inflation — Consumer Price Index releases
South African Reserve Bank

body.text: Inflation is measured in South Africa by Statistics South Africa through the Consumer Price Index (CPI), published monthly. It tracks how the price of a representative basket of goods and services changes over time. When you hear “inflation is 4,3%”, it means that basket costs about 4,3% more than it did a year earlier.

Inflation figures change every month. For the current number, check the Stats SA CPI release directly — the link is in the sources below. This article is about what the number means for you, which doesn't change month to month.
The part that matters if you have debt

Your debt repayments are usually fixed amounts. Your living costs are not. When prices rise and your income doesn't rise by the same amount, the gap comes out of the same place: whatever was left over each month.
That's why people often describe debt becoming “unmanageable” without having borrowed anything new. Nothing about the debt changed — the space around it shrank.
A simple illustration

Suppose you earn R18 000 after tax, your essential living costs are R11 000, and your debt repayments are R5 000. You have R2 000 of breathing room. If living costs rise by 6% over a year to roughly R11 660, and your income stays flat, that R2 000 becomes about R1 340 — a third less — with no change to your debt at all.
These are illustrative figures to show the mechanism, not a prediction about your situation.
Why averages can mislead

Headline inflation is an average across a broad basket. Your personal experience depends on what you actually spend money on. If most of your income goes to food, transport and electricity, and those categories rise faster than the average, your real cost increase can be higher than the headline figure suggests.
What you can actually do

items: Rebuild your budget from recent bank statements rather than memory — costs drift upward quietly.
Look at your total debt repayments as a share of take-home pay, and watch that share over time.
Deal with an unaffordable repayment structure early, while more options are still open.
Be wary of covering a shortfall with new short-term credit, which raises next month's fixed commitments.

body.text: When it stops being a budgeting problem

If essential living costs plus debt repayments consistently exceed your income, tightening the budget further has limits. That's the point at which it's worth having your actual numbers assessed rather than trying to absorb the gap indefinitely.

items.q: Where does South Africa's official inflation figure come from?
items.a: Statistics South Africa publishes the Consumer Price Index (CPI) monthly. It's the official measure of consumer inflation.

items.q: Does inflation increase what I owe?
items.a: Not directly. Your repayments are typically fixed amounts. Inflation reduces what's left of your income after living costs, which is what makes existing repayments harder to meet.

items.q: Is this article's example based on my situation?
items.a: No. The figures are illustrative, to show how the mechanism works. Use the budget calculator for a picture based on your own numbers.

title: How Interest Rates Affect Your Monthly Repayments
excerpt: Repo rate, prime rate, fixed versus linked — what actually moves your instalment, and which of your debts are exposed.

sources.title: South African Reserve Bank
National Credit Act 34 of 2005

body.text: Interest rate changes are reported as though everyone is affected equally. In practice, whether a rate change reaches your bank account depends on the kind of credit agreements you hold.
Repo rate and prime rate

The South African Reserve Bank sets the repo rate — the rate at which it lends to commercial banks. Banks price their lending off that, and the prime rate is the benchmark most consumer lending is quoted against, usually as “prime plus” some margin based on your risk profile.
When the repo rate moves, prime typically moves with it, and credit linked to prime follows.
Which of your debts actually move

items: Home loans: usually linked to prime, so instalments move when rates move.
Vehicle finance: depends on the agreement — some are linked, some fixed.
Credit cards and store accounts: rates vary, and are often already near the maximum permitted.
Personal loans: frequently fixed for the term, so an existing loan's instalment may not change.

body.text: If you're unsure which of yours are linked or fixed, the agreement itself says so. It's worth actually checking rather than assuming — people are often surprised in both directions.
Why a small percentage feels big

On long-term debt, a small rate change applies to a large outstanding balance for many years, so the effect on the monthly instalment is more noticeable than the percentage sounds. On a short-term loan that's nearly repaid, the same change barely registers.
Rate caps exist

The National Credit Act and its regulations prescribe maximum interest rates for different categories of credit agreement. A credit provider cannot charge whatever it likes. If you believe you're being charged beyond what's permitted, that is something to raise — with the provider, and if unresolved, with the regulator.
What to do when rates rise

Recalculate your budget with the new instalment rather than waiting to see whether you cope. If the new total pushes your repayments past what your income can carry alongside essential expenses, that is worth addressing early rather than after arrears build up.

items.q: Who sets interest rates in South Africa?
items.a: The South African Reserve Bank sets the repo rate. Banks set their own lending rates off that, with prime as the common benchmark.

items.q: Will a rate cut reduce all my repayments?
items.a: Only on agreements linked to a variable rate such as prime. Fixed-rate agreements keep the same instalment.

items.q: Is there a limit on what interest I can be charged?
items.a: Yes. The National Credit Act and its regulations prescribe maximum rates for different categories of credit agreement.

title: How Do I Know If I Am Over-Indebted?
excerpt: Over-indebtedness has a specific legal meaning in South Africa — and some practical warning signs that usually show up well before it does.

sources.title: National Credit Act 34 of 2005
Notebook on the National Credit Act, 2005
sources.publisher: Department of Trade, Industry and Competition

body.text: “Over-indebted” isn't just a description of feeling stretched. Under the National Credit Act it's a specific finding — and it covers more than being unable to pay today.
The legal meaning

Section 79 of the National Credit Act frames over-indebtedness in terms of whether a consumer is or will be unable to satisfy their obligations under all their credit agreements in a timely manner. Importantly, it extends beyond an existing inability to a future or imminent one — you do not have to already be in default.
A debt counsellor makes a determination on this after assessing your income, expenses and debts. A court then declares over-indebtedness and grants relief.
Practical warning signs

items: You use credit to cover ordinary monthly expenses like food, fuel or electricity.
You take new credit largely to service existing credit.
You pay minimums on revolving accounts and the balance never really falls.
You're juggling which account to skip each month.
Essential expenses plus debt repayments exceed take-home pay, so any shortfall is financed.

body.text: None of these individually proves anything. A pattern of them, sustained over months, is usually a structural problem rather than a run of bad months.
A rough self-check

Add your take-home pay. Subtract essential living costs. Subtract total monthly debt repayments. If the result is consistently negative or near zero with no buffer, you're relying on something to go right every month — which is precisely what fails when a car needs repairs or a medical cost appears.
The budget calculator on this site does this arithmetic for you and gives you a summary. It's a general budget picture, not a formal assessment.
Why acting early matters

Because over-indebtedness under the Act includes a future inability to pay, you don't have to wait until accounts are in arrears to seek help. Earlier generally means more options remain open — once matters reach judgment stage, the range of realistic outcomes narrows.

items.q: Do I have to be behind on payments to be over-indebted?
items.a: No. Section 79 of the NCA covers a future or imminent inability to meet obligations, not only an existing one.

items.q: Can I decide myself that I'm over-indebted?
items.a: You can recognise the signs, but the finding follows an assessment by a debt counsellor and a declaration by a court.

items.q: Does the calculator tell me if I qualify for debt review?
items.a: No. It gives a general budget summary. Qualifying requires a full assessment of your circumstances.
